title: Introductory Chapter
paragraphs: Of all the new things that caught my attention during my stay in the United States, none struck me more forcibly than the general equality of conditions. I quickly saw the enormous influence this fundamental fact exerts on the whole course of society: it gives a particular direction to public opinion, a particular character to the laws, new principles to those who govern, and distinctive habits to those who are governed. I soon perceived that this fact reaches far beyond the country's politics and laws — it rules civil society just as thoroughly as it rules the government. It creates opinions, generates sentiments, shapes the ordinary practices of daily life, and alters even what it does not itself produce. The further I advanced in the study of American society, the more I recognized that equality of conditions is the fundamental fact from which all others seem to derive, and the central point at which all my observations constantly converged.

I then turned my thoughts to our own hemisphere, where I seemed to detect something analogous to what the New World had shown me. I noticed that equality of conditions is advancing daily toward those extreme limits it appears to have reached in the United States, and that the democracy that governs American communities is rapidly rising toward power in Europe. From this observation came the idea for the book now before the reader.

Everyone agrees that a great democratic revolution is underway among us, but opinions differ on its nature and consequences. Some see it as a recent accident that can still be stopped; others see it as irresistible, because it is the most uniform, the most ancient, and the most enduring tendency found in history. Consider the state of France seven hundred years ago, when the land was divided among a small number of families who owned the soil and ruled its inhabitants. The right to govern descended through family inheritance from one generation to the next; force was the only means by which one person could act upon another, and landed property was the sole source of power. Soon, however, the political power of the clergy was established and began to assert itself. The clergy opened its ranks to all classes — to the poor and the rich, the villein and the lord; equality entered the government through the Church, and the man who as a serf would have vegetated in perpetual bondage took his seat as a priest among nobles, and not infrequently above the heads of kings.

As society gradually became more stable and more civilized, the relations between men grew more complicated and more numerous. From this came the need for civil laws; and soon the order of legal officials rose from the obscurity of tribunals and their dusty chambers to appear at the monarch's court, beside the feudal barons in their ermine and their chain mail. While kings were ruining themselves with grand enterprises and nobles were exhausting their resources in private wars, the lower orders were enriching themselves through commerce. The influence of money began to be felt in affairs of state. Business transactions opened a new road to power, and the financier rose to a position of political influence where he was at once flattered and despised. Gradually the spread of learning and the growing taste for literature and art opened paths of success to talent: science became a means of government, intelligence brought social power, and the man of letters took part in the affairs of state. The value attached to the privileges of birth fell in exact proportion to the new paths opened for advancement. In the eleventh century, nobility was beyond all price; in the thirteenth, it could be purchased; it was first conferred as a grant in 1270 — and so equality was introduced into government by the aristocracy itself.

Over these seven hundred years, the nobles sometimes granted the people a share of political rights in order to resist the authority of the Crown or to weaken their rivals. More often, the king permitted the lower orders to enjoy some measure of power with the aim of suppressing the aristocracy. In France, the kings have always been the most active and the most consistent levelers. When they were strong and ambitious, they spared no effort to raise the people to the level of the nobles; when they were temperate or weak, they let the people rise above themselves. Some helped democracy through their talents, others through their vices. Louis XI and Louis XIV reduced every rank beneath the throne to the same subjection; Louis XV descended, himself and his whole Court, into the dust.

As soon as land was held on some basis other than feudal tenure, and personal property in its turn began to confer influence and power, every improvement in commerce or manufacture became a fresh element of equality. From that point on, every new discovery, every new want it generated, and every new desire demanding satisfaction was a step toward the universal level. The taste for luxury, the love of war, the sway of fashion, and the most superficial as well as the deepest passions of the human heart all cooperated to enrich the poor and impoverish the rich.

Once the exercise of intellect became a source of strength and wealth, every addition to science, every fresh truth, and every new idea had to be regarded as a seed of power placed within the people's reach. Poetry, eloquence, and memory, the grace of wit, the glow of imagination, the depth of thought — all the gifts that Providence bestows with an equal hand — turned to the advantage of democracy. Even when these gifts were held by democracy's adversaries, they still served its cause by throwing into relief the natural greatness of man. Democracy's conquests spread in step with those of civilization and knowledge, and literature became an arsenal where the poorest and weakest could always find weapons to their hand.

Reading through our history, we will hardly find a single great event in the last seven hundred years that has not turned to the advantage of equality. The Crusades and the wars with the English decimated the nobles and divided their possessions; the rise of communes introduced an element of democratic liberty into the heart of the feudal monarchy; the invention of firearms equalized villein and noble on the battlefield; printing gave the same resources to minds of every class; the postal system carried the same information to the poor man's cottage and to the palace gate; and Protestantism proclaimed that all men are equally capable of finding the road to heaven. The discovery of America opened a thousand new paths to fortune, and placed riches and power within reach of the adventurous and the obscure. If we examine what has happened in France at fifty-year intervals since the eleventh century, we will invariably see that a twofold revolution has taken place in society. The noble has descended the social ladder, and the roturier has risen; one falls as the other rises. Every half century brings them closer together, and very soon they will meet.

Nor is this phenomenon unique to France. Wherever we turn our eyes, we will see the same continual revolution throughout all of Christendom. In every nation, the various events of national life have turned to the advantage of democracy; all men have contributed to it by their efforts — those who intentionally worked in its cause and those who served it unwittingly, those who fought for it and those who declared themselves its opponents. All have been driven along the same track, all have labored toward the same end, some ignorantly and some unwillingly — all have been blind instruments in the hands of God.

The gradual development of the equality of conditions is therefore a providential fact, and it has all the characteristics of a divine decree: it is universal, it is enduring, it constantly eludes all human interference, and all events and all men contribute to its progress. Would it then be wise to imagine that a social impulse dating from so far back can be checked by the efforts of a single generation? Can we really believe that the democracy which has annihilated the feudal system and conquered kings will respect the citizen and the capitalist? Will it stop now that it has grown so strong and its adversaries so weak? No one can say where we are going, because all points of comparison are lacking: equality of conditions is more complete in today's Christian countries than it has ever been at any time or in any place in the world — and so the scale of what already exists prevents us from foreseeing what may yet come.

The entire book now offered to the public has been written under the impression of a kind of religious dread, produced in the author's mind by the contemplation of a revolution so irresistible — a revolution that has advanced for centuries in spite of astonishing obstacles, and that is still proceeding amid the ruins it has made. It is not necessary for God himself to speak in order to disclose to us the unquestionable signs of his will; we can discern them in the habitual course of nature, and in the invariable tendency of events. I know, without special revelation, that the planets move in the orbits traced by the Creator's finger. If the men of our time were led by careful observation and sincere reflection to acknowledge that the gradual, progressive development of social equality is at once the past and the future of their history, that single truth would confer the sacred character of a divine decree upon the change. To attempt to check democracy would then be to resist the will of God, and nations would be obliged to make the best of the social lot assigned to them by Providence.

The Christian nations of our age seem to me to present a most alarming spectacle. The impulse that bears them along is so strong that it cannot be stopped, but it is not yet so rapid that it cannot be guided: their fate is still in their hands — but only for a little while longer. The first duty imposed at this moment on those who direct our affairs is to educate the democracy: to warm its faith, if that is possible; to purify its morals; to direct its energies; to substitute knowledge of practical business for its inexperience, and an acquaintance with its true interests for its blind propensities; to adapt its government to time and place, and to modify it in response to the events and actors of the age. A new science of politics is indispensable to a new world. This, however, is what we think of least. Launched into the middle of a rapid stream, we obstinately fix our eyes on the ruins still visible on the shore we have left, while the current sweeps us along and drives us backward toward the gulf.

In no country in Europe has the great social revolution I have been describing made such rapid progress as in France; yet it has always been carried forward by chance. The heads of state have never shown any forethought for its demands, and its victories have been won without their consent or even their knowledge. The most powerful, the most intelligent, and the most moral classes of the nation have never tried to connect themselves with it in order to guide it. The people have consequently been abandoned to their wild propensities, and they have grown up like those outcasts who receive their education in the public streets and who know nothing but the vices and wretchedness of society. The existence of a democracy seemed unknown — until suddenly it took possession of the supreme power. Then everything was submitted to its caprices; it was worshipped as the idol of strength. When it was at last enfeebled by its own excesses, the legislator conceived the rash project of annihilating its power instead of instructing it and correcting its vices. No attempt was made to fit it to govern: all efforts were bent on excluding it from government.

The consequence has been that the democratic revolution has been accomplished only in the material parts of society, without the corresponding change in laws, ideas, customs, and manners that was necessary to make such a revolution beneficial. We have gotten a democracy, but without the conditions that lessen its vices and bring out its natural advantages. And although we already see the evils it brings, we remain ignorant of the benefits it may yet confer.

While the power of the Crown, supported by the aristocracy, peacefully governed the nations of Europe, society possessed — amid its wretchedness — several advantages that can now scarcely be appreciated or imagined. The power of one part of his subjects was an insurmountable barrier to the prince's tyranny; and the monarch, feeling the almost divine character he enjoyed in the eyes of the multitude, drew a motive for the just use of his power from the respect he inspired. As high as they stood above the people, the nobles could not help taking that calm and benevolent interest in the people's fate that a shepherd feels toward his flock; and without acknowledging the poor as their equals, they watched over the destiny of those whose welfare Providence had entrusted to their care. The people, never having conceived of a social condition different from their own and never expecting to rank with their chiefs, received benefits from them without disputing their rights. The people grew attached to them when they were merciful and just, and submitted without resistance or servility to their exactions, as to the inevitable visitations of the arm of God. Custom and the manners of the time had also created a kind of law in the midst of violence, and set certain limits to oppression. Since the noble never suspected that anyone would try to deprive him of the privileges he believed to be legitimate, and since the serf regarded his own inferiority as a consequence of the immutable order of nature, it is easy to imagine that a mutual exchange of goodwill took place between two classes so differently gifted by fate. Inequality and wretchedness existed in society then — but the souls of neither class were degraded. Men are not corrupted by the exercise of power or debased by the habit of obedience; they are corrupted by the exercise of a power they believe to be illegal, and by obedience to a rule they consider to be usurped and oppressive. On one side was wealth, strength, and leisure, accompanied by the refinements of luxury, the elegance of taste, the pleasures of wit, and the religion of art. On the other was labor and a rude ignorance — and yet, amid this coarse and ignorant multitude, it was not uncommon to meet with energetic passions, generous sentiments, profound religious convictions, and independent virtues. A body politic so organized could boast of its stability, its power, and above all its glory.

But the scene has now changed. Gradually the two ranks mingle; the divisions that once separated mankind are lowered, property is divided, power is held in common, the light of learning spreads, and the capacities of all classes are equally cultivated. The state becomes democratic, and the empire of democracy is slowly and peacefully introduced into the institutions and manners of the nation. I can conceive of a society in which all men would profess an equal attachment and respect for the laws of which they are the common authors — in which the authority of the state would be respected as necessary, though not as divine, and the citizen's loyalty to the chief magistrate would not be a passion but a quiet, rational persuasion. Every individual possessing rights he is sure to retain, a kind of manly reliance and reciprocal courtesy would arise between all classes, alike free from pride and meanness. The people, well acquainted with their true interests, would acknowledge that to enjoy the advantages of society it is necessary to meet its demands. In this state of things, the voluntary association of citizens might replace the individual exertions of the nobles, and the community would be equally protected from anarchy and from oppression.

I admit that in a democratic state thus constituted, society will not be stationary — but the impulses of the social body can be regulated and directed forward. If there is less splendor than in the halls of an aristocracy, the contrast of misery will also be less frequent. The pleasures of enjoyment may be less excessive, but those of comfort will be more general. The sciences may be less perfectly cultivated, but ignorance will be less common. The impetuosity of the feelings will be restrained, and the habits of the nation softened; there will be more vices and fewer crimes. In the absence of enthusiasm and ardent faith, great sacrifices may be obtained from the members of a commonwealth by an appeal to their understanding and experience. Each individual will feel the same necessity of uniting with his fellow-citizens to protect his own weakness; and knowing that if they are to help him, he must cooperate with them, he will readily see that his personal interest is identified with the community's. The nation, taken as a whole, will be less brilliant, less glorious, and perhaps less strong; but the majority of citizens will enjoy a greater degree of prosperity, and the people will remain quiet — not because they despair of improvement, but because they are conscious of the advantages of their condition. If not all the consequences of this state of things would be good or useful, society would at least have appropriated those that are good and useful; and having once and for all renounced the social advantages of aristocracy, mankind would enter into possession of all the benefits democracy can offer.

But here it may be asked what we have adopted in place of the institutions, ideas, and customs of our forefathers that we have abandoned. The spell of royalty is broken, but it has not been succeeded by the majesty of the laws. The people have learned to despise all authority — but fear now extorts a larger tribute of obedience than reverence and love once did.

I see that we have destroyed those independent beings which were able to cope with tyranny single-handed — but it is the Government that has inherited the privileges of which families, corporations, and individuals have been deprived. The weakness of the whole community has thus replaced the influence of a small body of citizens, which, if it was sometimes oppressive, was often conservative. The division of property has lessened the distance separating the rich from the poor; but it seems that the nearer they draw to each other, the greater their mutual hatred, and the more vehement the envy and dread with which they resist each other's claims to power. The notion of Right is equally alien to both classes, and Force offers each the only argument for the present and the only guarantee for the future. The poor man keeps the prejudices of his ancestors without their faith, and their ignorance without their virtues; he has adopted the doctrine of self-interest as the rule of his actions without understanding the science that governs it, and his egotism is no less blind than his devotion once was. If society is tranquil, it is not because it relies on its strength and well-being, but because it knows its weakness and infirmities; a single effort may cost it its life. Everyone feels the evil, but no one has courage or energy enough to seek the cure. The desires, regrets, sorrows, and joys of the time produce nothing visible or permanent — like the passions of old men, which end in impotence.

We have, then, abandoned whatever advantages the old state of things offered, without receiving any compensation from our present condition. We have destroyed an aristocracy, and we seem inclined to survey its ruins with complacency, and to take up our abode in the midst of them.

The phenomena of the intellectual world are no less deplorable. The democracy of France, checked in its course or abandoned to its lawless passions, has overthrown whatever crossed its path and has shaken everything it has not destroyed. Its empire over society was not gradually introduced or peaceably established, but has constantly advanced amid disorder and the agitation of conflict. In the heat of the struggle, each partisan is driven beyond the limits of his own opinions by the opinions and excesses of his opponents, until he loses sight of the goal of his exertions and adopts a language that disguises his real sentiments or secret instincts. Hence the strange confusion we are witnessing. I cannot recall a passage in history more worthy of sorrow and pity than the scenes now playing out before our eyes. It is as if the natural bond that once united a man's opinions to his tastes and his actions to his principles has now been broken; the sympathy always acknowledged between human feelings and ideas appears dissolved, and all the laws of moral analogy abolished.

Zealous Christians can be found among us whose minds are nurtured in the love and knowledge of a future life, and who readily embrace the cause of human liberty as the source of all moral greatness. Christianity, which has declared that all men are equal in the sight of God, will not refuse to acknowledge that all citizens are equal in the eye of the law. But by a singular concourse of events, religion has become entangled in the very institutions democracy assails, and so is not infrequently led to reject the equality it loves, and to curse as an enemy a cause of liberty it might instead sanctify by its alliance.

Beside these religious men I see others whose eyes are turned more to the earth than to Heaven. They are partisans of liberty, not only as the source of the noblest virtues, but especially as the root of all solid advantages; and they sincerely want to extend its reach and impart its blessings to mankind. It would be natural for them to hasten to invoke the aid of religion — for they must know that liberty cannot be established without morality, nor morality without faith. But they have seen religion in the ranks of their adversaries, and they inquire no further. Some of them attack it openly, and the rest are afraid to defend it.

In former ages, slavery was advocated by the venal and slavish-minded, while the independent and the warm-hearted struggled without hope to save the liberties of mankind. But now one meets men of high and generous character whose opinions are at odds with their inclinations, and who praise a servility they have themselves never known. Others, by contrast, speak in the name of liberty as if they could feel its sanctity and its majesty, and loudly claim for humanity those rights they have always disowned. There are virtuous and peaceful individuals whose pure morality, quiet habits, affluence, and talents fit them to be leaders of the surrounding population. Their love of country is sincere, and they are prepared to make the greatest sacrifices for its welfare — but they confuse the abuses of civilization with its benefits, and the idea of evil is inseparable in their minds from that of novelty.

Not far from this class is another party, whose aim is to materialize mankind — to hit upon what is expedient without heeding what is just, to acquire knowledge without faith, and prosperity without virtue. They assume the title of champions of modern civilization, and take up a station they usurp with insolence and from which they are driven by their own unworthiness. Where does this leave us? The religionists are the enemies of liberty, and the friends of liberty attack religion; the high-minded and the noble advocate subjection, while the meanest and most servile minds preach independence; honest and enlightened citizens oppose all progress, while men without patriotism and without principles are the apostles of civilization and intelligence. Has such been the fate of the centuries that preceded ours? Has man always inhabited a world like the present, where nothing is linked together, where virtue is without genius and genius without honor — where the love of order is confused with a taste for oppression, and the holy rites of freedom with a contempt for law; where the light that conscience throws on human actions is dim, and where nothing any longer seems forbidden or allowed, honorable or shameful, false or true? I cannot, however, believe that the Creator made man only to leave him in an endless struggle with the intellectual miseries that surround us. God destines a calmer and a more certain future to the communities of Europe. I am unacquainted with his designs, but I shall not stop believing in them because I cannot fathom them; I would rather mistrust my own capacity than his justice.

There is one country in the world where the great revolution I am speaking of seems almost to have reached its natural limits. It has been accomplished there with ease and simplicity — or rather, that country has attained the consequences of the democratic revolution we are undergoing without having gone through the revolution itself. The emigrants who settled on the shores of America at the beginning of the seventeenth century separated the democratic principle from all the principles that repressed it in the old communities of Europe, and transplanted it unalloyed to the New World. There it has been allowed to spread in perfect freedom, and to work out its consequences in the laws by influencing the manners of the country.

It appears to me beyond doubt that sooner or later we shall arrive, as the Americans have, at an almost complete equality of conditions. But I do not conclude from this that we shall necessarily be led to draw the same political consequences the Americans have drawn from a similar social organization. I am far from supposing that they have chosen the only form of government a democracy may adopt; but the shared cause of laws and manners in the two countries is enough to explain the immense interest we have in becoming acquainted with its effects in each of them.

It is not, then, merely to satisfy a legitimate curiosity that I have examined America; my wish has been to find lessons we may ourselves profit from. Anyone who imagines that I have intended to write a panegyric will see that this was not my design. Nor has it been my aim to advocate any particular form of government, for I believe that absolute excellence is rarely to be found in any legislation. I have not even affected to discuss whether the social revolution, which I believe to be irresistible, is advantageous or harmful to mankind. I have acknowledged this revolution as a fact already accomplished or on the eve of its accomplishment; and I have selected the nation, from among those that have undergone it, in which its development has been the most peaceful and complete, in order to discern its natural consequences and, if possible, identify the means by which it may be made profitable. I confess that in America I saw more than America: I sought the image of democracy itself, with its inclinations, its character, its prejudices, and its passions — in order to learn what we have to fear or to hope from its progress.

In the first part of this work I have tried to show the tendency given to the laws by the democracy of America — a democracy abandoned almost without restraint to its instinctive propensities — and to exhibit the course it prescribes to government and the influence it exercises on public affairs. I have sought to discover the evils and the advantages it produces. I have examined the precautions the Americans use to direct it, as well as those they have not adopted, and I have undertaken to point out the causes that enable it to govern society. I do not know whether I have succeeded in making known what I saw in America, but I am certain that this has been my sincere desire, and that I have never knowingly molded facts to ideas, rather than ideas to facts.

Wherever a point could be established from written documents, I had recourse to the original text and to the most authentic and approved works. I have cited my authorities in the notes, and anyone may consult them. Wherever an opinion, a political custom, or a remark on the country's manners was concerned, I tried to consult the most enlightened men I met. If the point was important or doubtful, I was not satisfied with one witness but formed my opinion on the testimony of several. Here the reader must necessarily take me at my word. I could often have quoted names known to him, or deserving to be, in proof of what I claim; but I have carefully abstained from this practice. A stranger often hears important truths at the fireside of his host — truths the host would perhaps hide from the ear of a friend. He consoles himself with his guest for the silence imposed on him, and the shortness of the traveler's stay removes all fear of indiscretion. I carefully noted every conversation of this kind as soon as it occurred, but these notes will never leave my writing-case. I would rather weaken the success of my statements than add my name to the list of strangers who repay generous hospitality with subsequent chagrin and annoyance.

I am aware that, despite my care, nothing will be easier than to criticize this book, if anyone ever chooses to. Readers who examine it closely will discover the fundamental idea that connects its several parts. But the diversity of subjects I have had to treat is exceedingly great, and it will not be hard to oppose an isolated fact to the body of facts I cite, or an isolated idea to the body of ideas I put forward. I hope to be read in the spirit that has guided my labors, and that my book will be judged by the general impression it leaves — for I have formed my own judgment not on any single reason, but on the mass of evidence. It must not be forgotten that an author who wishes to be understood is obliged to push all his ideas to their utmost theoretical consequences, often to the verge of what is false or impracticable. If it is sometimes necessary to depart from the rules of logic in active life, such is not the case in discourse: a man finds that almost as many difficulties arise from inconsistency of language as from inconsistency of conduct.

I conclude by pointing out for myself what many readers will consider the principal defect of the work. This book is written to favor no particular views, and in composing it I have entertained no intention of serving or attacking any party. I have undertaken not to see differently, but to look further than parties; while they are busy with tomorrow, I have turned my thoughts to the Future.
